pictures.find: histogram unequal class widths frequency density
pictures.alt: A histogram with bars of different widths

lessons.title: Drawing histograms
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we draw a histogram that tells the truth?
objectives: To understand how to construct a histogram with unequal class widths
successCriteria: All: complete a frequency density column
Most: draw a histogram with a correct scale, touching bars and labelled axes
Some: check a histogram by adding bar areas
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: histograms of seedling growth from a home experiment
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah has counted all things in number (Surat al-Jinn 72:28)

keywords.def: bars touching, area showing frequency
evenly spaced numbers on an axis
where one class ends and the next begins
frequency ÷ class width

hook.text: Two pupils draw histograms from the same data, but one uses frequency on the vertical axis. How could you tell whose is misleading?
hook.a: Check the areas: in a true histogram width × height gives each frequency, and the total area gives the total.

starter.q: Write the class width of 4 < h ≤ 6.

teach.heading: The data
teach.note: Pupils fill in the last column first.

teach.heading: Drawing steps
bullets: Bars touch; widths match the classes
teach.note: Model on squared paper: 1 cm for 2 cm of height, 1 cm for 1 unit of density.

model.problem: Draw the bar for 4 < h ≤ 6.

teach.heading: Check by area
bullets: Add width × height of every bar
It should equal the total frequency

model.problem: Check the seedling histogram.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Ask: why must the bars touch? (the data is continuous).

misconception.wrong: Vertical axis labelled 'Frequency' with gaps between bars
misconception.right: Label it 'Frequency density'; bars touch because the data is continuous

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Which vertical axis label is correct for a histogram with unequal class widths?
check.why: Height is frequency density so that area shows frequency.

practice.q: Find the frequency density for 0 < h ≤ 4 (frequency 6).
practice.model: Class width 4 − 0 = 4. Frequency density = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. The bar runs from 0 to 4, height 1.5.

practice.q: Find the frequency density for 6 < h ≤ 8 (frequency 14).
Find the frequency density for 12 < h ≤ 20 (frequency 8).
What is the total area of the seedling histogram?

independent.q: Core: Draw a histogram of journey times: 0 < t ≤ 10: 5; 10 < t ≤ 20: 15; 20 < t ≤ 25: 20; 25 < t ≤ 30: 12; 30 < t ≤ 50: 8.
independent.a: Frequency densities 0.5, 1.5, 4, 2.4, 0.4; bars touch; axis labelled frequency density
independent.model: Widths 10, 10, 5, 5, 20. Frequency densities: 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5; 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5; 20 ÷ 5 = 4; 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4; 8 ÷ 20 = 0.4. Scale 0 to 50 across, 0 to 4 up; bars touching.

independent.q: Extend: From your histogram, estimate the number of journeys between 22 and 27 minutes.
Stretch: Show that the total area of your histogram is 60.

exit.q: A class 8 < x ≤ 14 has frequency 30. How tall is its bar?
Big question: what makes a histogram honest?
exit.a: Bar areas are proportional to frequency, with frequency density on the vertical axis.

lessons.homework: Grow cress or bean seedlings on damp kitchen paper for a week (written guide in the portal), measure 20 of them and draw a histogram with unequal classes.
lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn axes with scales. EAL: 'touching', 'label', 'scale'. Stretch: choose your own unequal classes for a raw data set and justify them.

lessons.title: Comparing distributions: averages and spread
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we compare two sets of data fairly?
objectives: To understand how to compare distributions using an average and a measure of spread in context

Some: choose the best measures and explain why

keywords.def: how data is spread out
a typical value, such as the median
how varied the data is, such as the IQR
having little spread

hook.text: Class A's median test score is 62 with an IQR of 18. Class B's median is 55 with an IQR of 9. Which class did better? Is there more than one answer?
hook.a: A scored higher on average; B's scores were more consistent. A full comparison mentions both.

teach.heading: Two comparisons
bullets: One about the average, one about the spread
Each in the context of the question
teach.note: Mark schemes give a mark for each comparison in context.

teach.heading: Model answer
bullets: Compare, give the numbers, say what it means
teach.note: Write it on the board as a model paragraph.

model.problem: Compare the test scores of Class A and Class B.
steps: Average: A's median (62) is higher than B's (55), so A scored higher on average
Spread: B's IQR (9) is smaller than A's (18), so B's scores were more consistent
model.answer: Two comparisons, each with numbers and context

teach.heading: Choosing measures
bullets: Median and IQR are not affected by extreme values
The range uses only the two extremes
teach.note: With outliers, prefer median and IQR.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Ask: does a bigger IQR mean better scores?

misconception.wrong: B's IQR is smaller, so B did worse
misconception.right: A smaller IQR means more consistent, not better or worse on average

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Teams poll: launch it, give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: Which statement compares spread?
options: B's scores were more consistent (IQR 9 against 18)
check.why: IQR measures spread. A higher median compares averages.

practice.q: Delivery firm X: median 34 min, IQR 16. Firm Y: median 41 min, IQR 7. Compare the medians in context.
practice.a: X's median is lower, so X's deliveries were quicker on average
practice.model: Compare the medians with numbers and context: X's median (34 min) is lower than Y's (41 min), so X's deliveries were quicker on average.

practice.q: Compare the IQRs in context.
practice.a: Y's IQR is smaller, so Y's delivery times were more consistent

practice.q: Which firm would you choose if you need a reliable time? Why?
practice.a: Y: its times vary less, even though they are longer on average

practice.q: Which measure of spread ignores extreme values?

independent.q: Core (exam style, 2 marks): Year 10 homework times: median 30 min, IQR 17.4 min. Year 11: median 36 min, LQ 31 min, UQ 40 min. Compare the two distributions.
independent.a: Year 11's median is higher, so Year 11 took longer on average (B1). Year 11's IQR is 9, smaller than 17.4, so Year 11's times were more consistent (B1).
independent.model: Average: Year 11's median (36 min) is higher than Year 10's (30 min), so Year 11 took longer on average. Spread: Year 11's IQR is 40 − 31 = 9 min, less than 17.4 min, so Year 11's times were more consistent.

independent.q: Extend: A data set of journey times includes one value of 3 hours caused by a breakdown. Which average and spread should you use, and why?
independent.a: Median and IQR: they are not affected by the extreme value, unlike the mean and range.

independent.q: Stretch: Write a full comparison of two plant groups: Group P median 34.7 cm, IQR 16 cm; Group Q median 31 cm, IQR 22 cm.
independent.a: P's plants were taller on average (34.7 > 31). P's heights were more consistent (IQR 16 < 22).

exit.q: Median 48 and IQR 12 against median 52 and IQR 20. Write one comparison of spread in context (test scores).
exit.a: The first set of scores was more consistent (IQR 12 < 20).

exit.q: Big question: what does a fair comparison of two data sets need?
exit.a: An average and a measure of spread, each compared with numbers and explained in context.

(a) Draw the speed-time graph [2] (b) Find the acceleration [2] (c) Find the deceleration [1] (d) Find the total distance [3] (e) Find the average speed [2]
independent.model:
(d) Trapezium: parallel sides 40 s (the whole time) and 20 s (the top), height 24:
½ × (40 + 20) × 24 = 720 m (M1 M1 A1).

independent.q: Extend (3 marks): A train slows steadily from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over 400 m. How long does it take?
Stretch (3 marks): For the car in the Core question, after how many seconds has it travelled 300 m?
independent.a: 96 m in the first 8 s; 204 m more at 24 m/s takes 8.5 s: t = 16.5 s

exit.q: The area under a speed-time graph gives the:
A gradient of 0 on a speed-time graph means
Big question: how can the area under a graph be a distance?
exit.a: Speed × time = distance; for a rectangle that is the area, and triangles and trapezia extend it to changing speeds.

Test (1, 1): 1 + 2 = 3 ≤ 6, so x + 2y ≤ 6; with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

independent.q: Core (exam-style, 9 marks): A region R is bounded by the solid lines y = 1, y = x and x + y = 8. (a) Write the three inequalities that define R [3] (b) Find the coordinates of the vertices of R [3] (c) Find the area of R [3]
independent.model:
(a) Test (4, 2), which is inside R: 2 ≥ 1, 2 ≤ 4 and 6 ≤ 8.
So y ≥ 1, y ≤ x and x + y ≤ 8 (B1 each).
(c) Base from (1, 1) to (7, 1) is 6; height from y = 1 to y = 4 is 3; ½ × 6 × 3 = 9.

independent.q: Extend (3 marks): Find the line through (4, 4) perpendicular to x + y = 8.

independent.q: Stretch (4 marks): The point (a, 3) lies in R. Find the range of values of a.
independent.a: 3 ≤ a (from y ≤ x) and a + 3 ≤ 8 (so a ≤ 5): 3 ≤ a ≤ 5

exit.q: The region above the solid line y = -x + 4 is:
A good test point when it is not on a line
Big question: how do you work back to the inequalities from a shaded region?
exit.a: Find each boundary's equation, then use a point inside the region to choose each sign, solid for ≤ or ≥ and dashed for < or >.
